c.tagline: A maze of souks, spice, and rooftop sunsets.

avoid.reason: No true no-go zones, but skip the unlit outer medina alleys and the Sidi Youssef Ben Ali fringe late at night, when getting lost invites hassle.
Jemaa el-Fnaa and the souks see pickpocketing, aggressive touts, henna-scam artists and 'false guide' scams, especially after dark.

hood_desc: The ancient walled old city, a maze of souks, riads, palaces and the famous Jemaa el-Fna square alive with performers and food stalls. Ideal for travelers who want to immerse themselves in traditional Marrakech, sights and sensory bustle.

The modern French-built district with wide boulevards, contemporary cafes, boutiques, galleries and a lively dining scene. Suits visitors wanting a more relaxed, cosmopolitan base with modern comforts.
An upmarket quarter of luxury hotels, gardens, nightclubs and casinos between the old and new towns. Best for travelers seeking upscale accommodation and nightlife close to the medina.

The historic southern part of the medina around the royal palaces and the Saadian Tombs, quieter and rich in monuments. Good for those wanting history and atmosphere with fewer crowds than the central souks.

A tranquil palm-grove district on the city's outskirts, dotted with luxury villas, resorts and spas among the palms. Perfect for travelers wanting a peaceful, resort-style retreat away from the medina bustle.
lodging: Radisson Blu Hotel Marrakech Carre Eden
Riad Le Bijou de Zahra Marrakech Kasbah

water.note: Officially treated but CDC/NHS advise visitors stick to bottled or filtered water.

transit.pay: City buses are run by ALSA; pay the driver in cash, about 5 MAD (~US$0.50) per ride, so carry small change. There is no transit card worth getting for a short visit. Airport bus L19 sells tickets on board (30 MAD, ~US$3).
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6am-10pm; there is no night service.
transit.note: Most visitors walk the medina and use petit taxis (insist on the meter or agree a price first); buses mainly help for Gueliz, the Palmeraie and the airport.

landmarks: Jemaa el-Fnaa

The pulsing heart of Marrakesh, this UNESCO-listed square erupts nightly into a theater of snake charmers, storytellers, and smoking food stalls. By day it's a market; by dusk it becomes one of the most electric public spaces on Earth.
Koutoubia Mosque

Marrakesh's tallest and most iconic minaret has watched over the city for nearly nine centuries, its intricate sandstone facade inspiring both the Giralda in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat. Its silhouette against a desert sunset is the quintessential Marrakesh postcard.
Bahia Palace

Wander through a 19th-century labyrinth of carved cedar ceilings, zellige tilework, and citrus-scented courtyards built to be 'the most beautiful palace of its time.' Every room reveals another layer of Andalusian and Moroccan craftsmanship.
Jardin Majorelle

This electric-blue garden oasis, restored by Yves Saint Laurent, is a jungle of cacti, bamboo, and cobalt pavilions tucked away from the medina's chaos. It's a serene, art-deco escape and one of the most photographed gardens in Africa.
Saadian Tombs

Hidden for centuries and rediscovered only in 1917, these opulent royal tombs shimmer with gold leaf, Italian marble, and honeycomb muqarnas ceilings. They're a hauntingly beautiful glimpse into 16th-century Saadian dynasty splendor.
Medina of Marrakesh (Souks)

Lose yourself in a maze of narrow alleys packed with lantern makers, spice pyramids, leather tanners, and rug weavers. Every turn offers a new burst of color, scent, and sound in this UNESCO World Heritage old town.
El Badi Palace

Now a majestic ruin of towering pisé walls and sunken orange-tree gardens, this once-legendary 16th-century palace hints at the extravagance of Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's golden age. Storks nest atop its crumbling ramparts, adding to its faded grandeur.
Ben Youssef Madrasa

Once North Africa's largest Islamic college, this beautifully restored madrasa dazzles with geometric stucco work, cedar carvings, and a tranquil central pool. Its intricate symmetry makes it a favorite for photographers.
Menara Gardens

A vast olive grove centered on a serene 12th-century reflecting pool, with the snow-capped Atlas Mountains as a backdrop. It's the perfect spot for a peaceful escape and one of Marrakesh's most classic mountain-and-water views.
Museum of Marrakesh (Dar Menebhi Palace)

Housed in a stunning restored palace with a giant central chandelier, this museum showcases Moroccan art, ceramics, and textiles beneath ornately carved ceilings. The building itself, with its lush courtyard, is as much the attraction as the exhibits.

train.note: Morocco has no international trains - the Algerian border has been closed for decades and there is no rail link to Mauritania - so every train from Marrakech is domestic. From Marrakech station on Avenue Hassan II, ONCF runs direct trains to Casablanca (about 3 hours), Rabat, Fez and Tangier, plus an overnight service to Tangier. The Al Boraq high-speed line does not reach Marrakech yet; change at Casablanca Voyageurs for it, though the extension south is under construction. Tickets are cheapest and easiest on ONCF's own site or the ONCF Voyages app.

bus.note: No scheduled international coach starts in Marrakech. Spain-Morocco coach services do exist - ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en/web/bus/home) runs routes that cross on the Algeciras-Tangier ferry - but they begin in Casablanca and cities further north, so from Marrakech you would first take a domestic bus or train up the coast. Within Morocco the reliable long-distance operators are CTM (https://www.ctm.ma/) and Supratours (https://www.supratours.ma/), which is run by ONCF and connects with train services; both have terminals near the railway station rather than at the chaotic Bab Doukkala stand. Supratours is the usual choice for Essaouira and the Agadir/Dakhla runs down the Atlantic coast.

ferry.note: Marrakech is far inland with no ferries; boats to Spain (Balearia, FRS, AML and others) sail from Tangier Ville and Tanger Med, a full day's train or bus ride north.
